summary.text: A black smoker is a type of hydrothermal vent on the seabed that looks like a black chimney sending out a cloud of black material.
What pours out is mostly particles rich in sulfur-bearing minerals, known as sulfides.
Black smokers deliver a wide range of elements to the world's oceans, contributing to global marine biogeochemistry.

facts.label: Usual zone
facts.value: The bathyal zone, sometimes the deeper abyssal zone

items.prompt: A deep-sea robot films a dark chimney on the seafloor puffing out a black cloud. What is that cloud mostly made of?

options.label: Soot from rocks burning underwater
Particles rich in sulfur minerals
Ash from a nearby volcanic blast
Mud stirred up by deep currents

items.explain: Black smokers give off particles loaded with sulfur-bearing minerals, called sulfides, which make the cloud look dark.

items.prompt: Why does a vent chimney like a black smoker keep getting taller?

options.label: Lava oozes up and hardens around the opening
Sea animals build shells on top of each other
Dissolved minerals drop out when hot water meets cold
Currents pile seafloor sand against the vent

items.explain: Minerals dissolved in the superheated vent water come out as particles when it hits near-freezing seawater, and those particles add to the stack.

items.prompt: The seawater around deep vents is only about 2 °C. How hot can the water coming out of them get?

options.label: About 40 °C
Just under 100 °C
About 1,200 °C
Up to 464 °C

items.explain: Vent water has been measured from 60 °C up to as high as 464 °C, against roughly 2 °C for the water around it.

items.prompt: Vent water far above 100 °C can still stay liquid instead of boiling into steam. What makes that possible?

options.label: The huge water pressure at those depths
The cold seawater cooling it instantly
The salt making the water too heavy to boil
The darkness of the deep ocean floor

items.explain: The high pressure of the water above means vent water can stay liquid, or become a supercritical fluid, at such temperatures.

items.prompt: Giant tube worms, clams and shrimp crowd around a deep vent. What sits at the base of their food chain?

options.label: Seaweed growing on the chimney walls
Dead plankton sinking from the surface
Microbes that live off vent chemicals
Small fish that the worms hunt

items.explain: Chemosynthetic bacteria and archaea, fed by chemicals dissolved in the vent fluid, form the base of the food chain there.

items.prompt: Hydrothermal vents such as black smokers exist on Earth because of which pair of conditions?

options.label: A strong magnetic field and a thick atmosphere
Geologic activity and lots of water in and on the crust
Warm climates and very salty ocean water
A large Moon and strong ocean tides

items.explain: Vents form because Earth is geologically active and also has large amounts of water on its surface and inside its crust.

paragraphs.heading: What a black smoker is
paragraphs.text: A black smoker is one kind of hydrothermal vent, a crack in the seabed that lets out water heated from within the Earth. Up close, it looks like a dark chimney giving off a cloud of black material. That cloud is made of particles loaded with sulfur-bearing minerals, which are called sulfides. Vents can also form paler features known as white smokers.

paragraphs.heading: Where they are found
paragraphs.text: Black smokers usually sit in the bathyal zone, and they are most common between 2,500 and 3,000 m below the surface. Some are found in shallower water, and some lie deeper still, in the abyssal zone. Deep-ocean vents typically form along mid-ocean ridges, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge and the East Pacific Rise among them. These are places where two tectonic plates move apart and new crust is made.

paragraphs.heading: How the chimney grows
paragraphs.text: The water leaving a vent is mostly seawater, drawn in near the volcano through faults, porous sediment or volcanic rock, plus some water given off by upwelling magma. It carries minerals dissolved in it. When this superheated water meets the near-freezing sea, the minerals come out as particles that pile up and make the stack taller. A chimney begins with a layer of the mineral anhydrite. Sulfides of copper, iron and zinc then fill its gaps, so the wall grows less porous over time.

paragraphs.heading: Fast and tall
paragraphs.text: Vent chimneys can grow quickly: growth of about 30 cm in a single day has been recorded. Some reach 60 m in height. One towering vent nicknamed "Godzilla", on the deep Pacific seafloor near Oregon, rose to 40 m before it toppled in 1996.

paragraphs.heading: Hot water under pressure
paragraphs.text: The surrounding water at these depths is around 2 °C, yet vent water comes out at anywhere from 60 °C up to 464 °C. The huge pressure of the water at such depths means it can stay liquid at that heat, or become a supercritical fluid, with properties between those of a gas and a liquid. For seawater, venting is supercritical above 407 °C and 298.5 bars, a pressure found about 2,960 m below sea level.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Black and white smokers carry many different elements out into the world's oceans, and so help shape the chemistry of the global sea. The areas around vents are more productive than most of the deep sea. Bacteria and archaea there form the base of a food chain that runs on chemicals dissolved in the vent fluid, supporting giant tube worms, clams, limpets and shrimp. Some scientists have proposed that vents like these helped life get started.
